title: Neighbors and Building
intro: In a long outage the help that arrives first comes from the people on your own floor. This module takes you from swapping a few phone numbers to a floor that checks on its members, shares the heavy jobs and has a say in the building's plan. Any list of neighbors is kept on paper by the residents themselves, with each person's consent.

actions.title: Swap phone numbers with the neighbors on your floor
actions.why: In a long outage the people who can reach you fastest are the ones behind the nearest doors.
actions.how: Knock on the two or three doors closest to yours, say you are sorting out what to do in a power outage, and ask to swap names, unit numbers and cell numbers. Save theirs in your phone, then write them by hand on the printable floor contact list and keep it with your own papers.
actions.done: The names, unit numbers and cell numbers of two or three neighbors are saved in your phone and written on the floor contact list, and they have yours.

actions.title: Make a floor contact list, with buddies and one OK / HELP door sign
actions.why: A shared paper list, named buddies and one door sign let a floor check on everyone quickly, so nobody goes unchecked because everyone assumed someone else had knocked.
actions.how: Print the blank floor contact list and take it door to door, or bring it to a short get-together in the corridor or lobby. Each household writes its own line by hand: unit number, names, phone, email, any skills or equipment it is willing to share, and a role if it wants one. Ask each household two questions: would you like someone to check on you in an emergency, and what could you offer, such as first-aid training, a second language, strong legs for the stairs or a battery radio. People write only what they choose to, a yes is marked only when the person says yes, and paper copies go only to the households on the list. Pair each household with a buddy on the same floor, and name a second in case the first is away. Agree the trigger: after strong shaking, or once an outage has lasted longer than a time you set (for example 2 hours), each buddy knocks on the other's door, then once a day until services return. In extreme heat, check on anyone living alone several times a day, above all in the late afternoon and evening. Agree one door sign for the whole floor: a sheet with OK in large green letters on one side and HELP in red on the other, taped to the outside of each front door after an earthquake or in a long outage. Whoever walks the floor knocks at every door showing HELP and every door with no sign, starting with older neighbors and families with babies. Volunteers knock, carry and pass on messages; they are not first responders, and anything serious is a 911 call first.
actions.done: The floor contact list holds a line from each household that chose to join, with every yes, buddy and second marked, and each of those households holds a copy of the list and the OK / HELP sign.

actions.title: Find out who wants a knock on the door, and who can help
actions.why: Older people, people living alone, families with babies and anyone who cannot manage the stairs are the first to run short when the elevators and water stop.
actions.how: Ask every household on your list two questions: would you like someone to check on you in an emergency, and what could you offer, such as first-aid training, a second language, strong legs for the stairs or a battery radio. Mark the answers by hand on the floor contact list, and only when the person says yes. Agree that volunteers knock, carry and pass on messages, and call 911 for anything serious; they are not first responders.
actions.done: Each household on the list has answered both questions, and every yes is marked on the floor contact list.

actions.title: Pair up households as buddies
actions.why: A named buddy means nobody on the floor goes unchecked because everyone assumed someone else had knocked.
actions.how: Pair each household with one other on the same floor, and name a second in case the first is away. Agree the trigger: after strong shaking, or once an outage has lasted longer than a time you set (for example 2 hours), each buddy knocks on the other's door, then once a day until services return. In extreme heat, check on anyone living alone several times a day, above all in the late afternoon and evening. Write the pairs by hand on the floor contact list.
actions.done: Each household on the floor contact list has a buddy and a second written beside it, and every pair has agreed the trigger.

actions.title: Agree one OK / HELP door sign for the floor
actions.why: A sign on every door lets someone walking the corridor see in a minute who is fine and who needs a knock.
actions.how: Agree a single sign for the whole floor: a sheet of paper with OK in large green letters on one side and HELP in red on the other. After an earthquake or in a long outage, each household tapes or hangs it on the outside of its front door. Whoever walks the floor knocks at every door showing HELP and every door with no sign, starting with older neighbors and families with babies. The sign is for neighbors only; in a life-threatening emergency call 911 first.
actions.done: Each household on the floor that agreed holds the same sign, OK in green on one side and HELP in red on the other.

actions.title: Set up the building's plan, floor wardens, shared heavy jobs and a notice point
actions.why: A fire safety plan covers fire, but not who does what when the power, water or elevators are out for days.
actions.how: Write to your building manager, landlord, board or residents' association and ask whether a building-wide emergency plan exists besides the fire safety plan; if there is none, ask for it to go on the agenda of the next residents' or annual meeting. A useful plan names who can shut off the building's utilities, how residents will be told what is happening, a meeting place away from the building, and how residents who need help are checked on. At the meeting, propose one chief warden for the building and one or two volunteer wardens for each floor, each with a stand-in. Each floor warden keeps that floor's contact list, knows who has asked for a check, and passes messages between the floor and the chief warden. Wardens can link floors with two-way radios (CM-06 says which kinds need a license); test them in your building first, because concrete and distance cut the range. Wardens organize neighbors; they do not fight fires, attempt rescues or stand in for the fire department. On each floor, put at least two names against each of four jobs: carrying water and supplies up the stairs, bringing news from the lobby to every floor, knocking on the doors of people who asked for a check, and collecting handed-out supplies for the whole building in one trip. Match jobs to ability; someone who cannot climb can keep the list or mind children. With management's agreement, set one notice point in the lobby and one on each floor, such as the wall beside the elevator, never on fire doors, exit signs or fire equipment, and keep paper, tape and a thick marker there or with the floor warden. Every notice carries the date, the time and where the information came from, and is replaced at set times, for example 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Note management's answers on the Building information sheet, and the wardens and job names on each floor contact list.
actions.done: Management's answer about the plan is on the Building information sheet, each floor contact list names its wardens and two people for each heavy job, and the agreed notice points hold paper, tape and a marker.

actions.title: Propose floor wardens
actions.why: One known person on each floor gives residents and management a clear line for passing messages and checking doors.
actions.how: At a residents' meeting, propose one chief warden for the building and one or two volunteer wardens for each floor, each with a stand-in. Each floor warden keeps that floor's contact list, knows who has asked for a check, and passes messages between the floor and the chief warden. Wardens can link floors with two-way radios (CM-06 says which kinds need a license); test them in your building first, because concrete and distance cut the range. Wardens organize neighbors; they do not fight fires, attempt rescues or stand in for the fire department.
actions.done: The proposal has been made at a residents' meeting, and each warden and stand-in who said yes is named on their floor's contact list.

actions.title: Share out the heavy jobs before they are needed
actions.why: With the elevators out, getting water, supplies and news up many flights of stairs is too much for one household and manageable for a team.
actions.how: With your floor, put at least two names against each of four jobs: carrying water and supplies up the stairs, bringing news from the lobby to every floor, knocking on the doors of people who asked for a check, and collecting handed-out supplies for the whole building in one trip. Match jobs to ability; someone who cannot climb can keep the list or mind children. Write the names by hand on the floor contact list.
actions.done: Each of the four jobs has at least two names beside it on the floor contact list, and each named person has said yes.

actions.title: Set up a paper notice point
actions.why: When phones and the internet are down, one known spot for written notices cuts rumors and saves trips up and down the stairs.
actions.how: Agree one place in the lobby and one on each floor, such as the wall beside the elevator, where notices go up. Keep paper, tape and a thick marker there or with the floor warden. Every notice carries the date, the time and where the information came from, and is replaced at set times, for example 9 in the morning and 5 in the evening. Ask management before using a wall, and keep notices off fire doors, exit signs and fire equipment.
actions.done: Management has agreed the spots in the lobby and on each floor, and paper, tape and a thick marker are kept there or with the floor warden.

actions.title: Hold one stair walk or building drill a year
actions.why: Walking the route once a year finds locked doors, dead lights and people who cannot manage the stairs before a real emergency does.
actions.how: Pick a fixed date each year and tell management first. Everyone who is able walks their nearest stairwell from their own floor to the street and on to the meeting place, and someone times it. Anyone who cannot use the stairs practices their own plan: where they wait and who knocks. Report blocked landings, locked or propped doors and failed lights to management in writing the same day, and do not set off the alarm yourselves.
actions.done: The first walk has been held and timed, its date is fixed for next year, and anything blocked, locked or unlit was reported to management in writing.

actions.title: Take a class together
actions.why: A floor with two or three trained people can deal with injuries and small problems while emergency services are stretched.
actions.how: Ask who on the floor would join a first-aid and CPR class and book it as a group; many providers will teach a group on site. Ask your city or county emergency management office about Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) training, which covers fire safety, light search and rescue and disaster first aid. Note who has completed what on the floor contact list.
actions.done: The class has been held, and who completed what is noted on the floor contact list.

actions.title: Give new neighbors the basics in their first month
actions.why: Someone who moved in last week does not yet know the stairwells, the meeting place or who to ask.
actions.how: When someone moves onto your floor, knock within the first month and introduce yourself. Hand over one page listing the two nearest stairwells, the building's outside meeting place, the after-hours emergency number, when to flush with a bucket and when not to flush at all, what the OK / HELP door sign means and who the floor warden is. Offer them a line on the floor contact list to fill in by hand, and leave it to them whether they do.
actions.done: The one-page sheet for new neighbors is written with a spare copy ready, and the newest household on your floor has been handed one.
